{{nihongo|'''Tsuneko Okazaki'''|岡崎 恒子|Okazaki Tsuneko|extra=7 June 1933 – 22 September 2026}} was a Japanese pioneer of [[molecular biology]] known for her work on [[DNA replication]] and specifically for discovering [[Okazaki fragments]], along with her late husband [[Reiji Okazaki|Reiji]].<ref>{{cite book|title=The Complete Idiot's Guide to College Biology|year=2010|publisher=Penguin|isbn=978-1-59257-848-1|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=5n1w8K90G5UC&q=Tsuneko+Okazaki&pg=PT187| first =  Emily Jane | last = Willingham | name-list-style = vanc |access-date=6 January 2011}}</ref> She continued to be involved in academia, contributing to more advancements in DNA research.

== Early life and education ==
Tsuneko Okazaki was born in [[Nagoya]], capital of the [[Aichi Prefecture]] of Japan, on 7 June 1933.<ref>{{in lang|ja}}{{Cite web|url=https://brh.co.jp/s_library/interview/32/|title=『岡崎フラグメントと私』岡崎 恒子 {{!}} サイエンティスト・ライブラリー {{!}} JT生命誌研究館|website=サイエンティスト・ライブラリー {{!}} JT生命誌研究館|access-date=2016-05-15}}</ref><ref>{{cite web|url=https://archive.mith.umd.edu/gcr/text/text_1776586485.html|title=Gender, Race, and Class in Occupied Japan: Two Lives and the Double Helix}}</ref> She graduated from [[Aichi Prefectural Asahigaoka Senior High School]]. During her undergraduate years, she studied biology at [[Nagoya University of Arts and Sciences|Nagoya University School of Science]].<ref name=":0">{{cite journal | vauthors = Okazaki T | title = Days weaving the lagging strand synthesis of DNA - A personal recollection of the discovery of Okazaki fragments and studies on discontinuous replication mechanism | journal = Proceedings of the Japan Academy. Series B, Physical and Biological Sciences | volume = 93 | issue = 5 | pages = 322–338 | date = May 2017 | pmid = 28496054 | pmc = 5489436 | doi = 10.2183/pjab.93.020 | bibcode = 2017PJAB...93..322O }}</ref> She graduated with her PhD from the university  in 1956,<ref>{{Cite book|url=https://archive.org/details/biotechnology1010000shma|url-access=registration|title=Biotechnology 101|last=Shmaefsky|first=Brian | name-list-style = vanc | date = 2006 | publisher=Greenwood Publishing Group|isbn=9780313335280 }}</ref> which was also the year that she met her husband, Reiji Okazaki. They married that same year and soon after, they joined their research work and laboratories.<ref name=":0" />

== Work leading to and discovery of Okazaki fragments ==
Tsuneko and Reiji Okazaki's early research consisted of studying [[DNA synthesis]] and specific [[nucleotide]] characteristics in frog eggs and [[Sea urchin|sea urchins]].<ref name=":0" /> This work led to the discovery of thymidine-diphosphate rhamnose, a sugar-linked nucleotide, which then opened up the doors for them to work in the U.S. They worked at [[University of Washington]] and [[Stanford University]] in the labs of [[J. L. Strominger]] and [[Arthur Kornberg]], respectively, where there was a lot more availability of resources to further their research.<ref name=":0" /> Years later, after much research done in both the U.S and Japan, in 1968, Tsuneko and Reiji published their breakthrough findings on Okazaki fragments in [[Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences of the United States of America|''PNAS'']].<ref>{{cite journal | vauthors = Okazaki R, Okazaki T, Sakabe K, Sugimoto K, Sugino A | title = Mechanism of DNA chain growth. I. Possible discontinuity and unusual secondary structure of newly synthesized chains | journal = Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences of the United States of America | volume = 59 | issue = 2 | pages = 598–605 | date = February 1968 | pmid = 4967086 | pmc = 224714 | doi=10.1073/pnas.59.2.598| bibcode = 1968PNAS...59..598O | doi-access = free }}</ref> After Reiji Okazaki's early death from [[Little Boy|Hiroshima]]-induced [[leukemia]] in 1975, Tsuneko continued her research and moved on to proving the structure of the [[RNA]] primer associated with Okazaki fragments.<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://www.itbm.nagoya-u.ac.jp/okazaki_award/okazaki_fragment.html|title=Tsuneko & Reiji Okazaki Award - Okazaki Fragment|website=www.itbm.nagoya-u.ac.jp |access-date=2018-05-22}}</ref>

== Additional research contributions ==
Tsuneko continued to be involved in different research projects, mainly investigating different aspects of DNA. She served as head of laboratories, lead academic supervisor of students, and as a significant intellectual contributor. Specifically, her contributions have included research revealing hGCMa as a [[placenta]]-specific transcription regulator, possibly involved in the expression of multiple placenta-specific genes. She contributed to research on the human [[centromere]] protein B found to induce translational positioning of nucleosomes on α-satellite sequences.<ref>{{cite journal | vauthors = Suzuki N, Itou T, Hasegawa Y, Okazaki T, Ikeno M | title = Cell to cell transfer of the chromatin-packaged human beta-globin gene cluster | journal = Nucleic Acids Research | volume = 38 | issue = 5 | pages = e33 | date = March 2010 | pmid = 20007595 | pmc = 2836578 | doi = 10.1093/nar/gkp1168 }}</ref> She worked on understanding the [[Regulation of gene expression|genomic regulation]] of [[HLA-G]] and how the presence of a [[LINE1]] [[Gene silencing|gene silencer]] may explain the limited expression of HLA-G.<ref>{{cite journal | vauthors = Ikeno M, Suzuki N, Kamiya M, Takahashi Y, Kudoh J, Okazaki T | title = LINE1 family member is negative regulator of HLA-G expression | journal = Nucleic Acids Research | volume = 40 | issue = 21 | pages = 10742–52 | date = November 2012 | pmid = 23002136 | pmc = 3510505 | doi = 10.1093/nar/gks874 }}</ref> She also contributed to the research on mice with characteristics of [[down syndrome]] in order to understand the genotype-phenotype characteristics of down syndrome in humans.<ref>{{cite journal | vauthors = Miyamoto K, Suzuki N, Sakai K, Asakawa S, Okazaki T, Kudoh J, Ikeno M, Shimizu N | title = A novel mouse model for Down syndrome that harbor a single copy of human artificial chromosome (HAC) carrying a limited number of genes from human chromosome 21 | journal = Transgenic Research | volume = 23 | issue = 2 | pages = 317–29 | date = April 2014 | pmid = 24293126 | doi = 10.1007/s11248-013-9772-x | s2cid = 10330769 }}</ref>

== Career involvements ==
Tsuneko was an associate professor in molecular biology at the School of Science in Nagoya University from 1967 to 1983. She held this position until she became a lead professor from 1983 to 1997. In 1997, she moved to the Institute of Comprehensive Medical Science, [[Fujita Health University]], where she was a professor for five years and then became a visiting professor until 2008.<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Dijkstra |first1=Johannes M. |last2=Nagatsu |first2=Toshiharu |date=2024 |title=The Life and Science of Professor Tsuneko Okazaki, and her time at Fujita Health University |url=https://www.jstage.jst.go.jp/article/fmj/advpub/0/advpub_2023-014/_article |journal=Fujita Medical Journal |volume=advpub |issue=1 |pages=2023–014 |doi=10.20407/fmj.2023-014|pmid=38332776 |pmc=10847632 }}</ref> Additionally, throughout the years of 2004 to 2007, her main job was in the [[Stockholm]] office, where she was the director of the [[Japan Society for the Promotion of Science]]. She was also CEO/president and director of Chromo Research Inc. from 2008 to 2015.<ref name=":0" />

== Personal life and death ==
In 1963, after coming back from conducting research at [[University of Washington]] and [[Stanford University]] along with her husband, Tsuneko had her first child. She then had her second child in 1973. Due to the lack of nursery care in Japan at the time, Tsuneko had difficulty finding help to take care of her children, as she was working full-time with her research. She was part of a citizens' campaign where she marched for more availability of child-care support.<ref>{{Cite web|url=http://www.aip.nagoya-u.ac.jp/en/public/nu_research/features/detail/0003970.html|title=My Life & Okazaki Fragments {{!}} Features {{!}} Nagoya University Academic Research & Industry-Academia-Government Collaboration|website=Nagoya University Academic Research & Industry-Academia-Government Collaboration|language=ja|access-date=2018-05-22}}{{verify source |date=September 2023 |reason=This ref was deleted Special:Diff/846077352 by a bug in VisualEditor and later restored by a bot from the original cite located at Special:Permalink/844310883 cite #5 - verify the cite is accurate and delete this template. [[User:GreenC bot/Job 18]]}}</ref> Reiji Okazaki died in 1975, but Tsuneko continued working to complete the research they were working on.

Tsuneko died on 22 September 2026, at the age of 93.<ref>{{cite news|url=https://www.chunichi.co.jp/article/1322874|accessdate=11 October 2026|title=DNAの小さな断片「岡崎フラグメント」発見の岡崎恒子さん死去、93歳　名古屋大学特別教授|date=9 October 2026|language=ja|newspaper=[[Chunichi Shimbun]]}}</ref>

== Recognitions ==
Tsuneko was awarded [[Chunichi Culture Award]],<ref>{{Cite web|url=http://www.chunichi.co.jp/info/award/culture/page04.html|title=中日文化賞：第31回-第40回受賞者|publisher=中日新聞|accessdate=2009-10-26|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20100312001129/http://www.chunichi.co.jp/info/award/culture/page04.html|archive-date=2010-03-12|url-status=dead|language=ja}}</ref> the [[L'Oréal-UNESCO Awards for Women in Science]] in 2000.<ref>(2015-04-05)
 [http://www.thefreelibrary.com/DNA+researcher+Okazaki+wins+int'l+award+for+female+scientists.-a058678129 DNA researcher Okazaki wins int'l award for female scientists.], the Free Library, Retrieved 2017-10-31.</ref>

She was also awarded the [[Medals of Honor (Japan)|Medal with Purple Ribbon]] in 2000, the [[Order of the Sacred Treasure]], [and] [[Order of the Rising Sun|Gold Rays with Neck Ribbon]] in 2008.<ref name=":1">{{Cite web|url=http://www.aip.nagoya-u.ac.jp/en/public/nu_research/features/detail/0003970.html|title=My Life & Okazaki Fragments {{!}} Features {{!}} Nagoya University Academic Research & Industry-Academia-Government Collaboration|website=Nagoya University Academic Research & Industry-Academia-Government Collaboration|language=ja|access-date= 2018-05-22 }}</ref>

In 2015, [[Nagoya University]] created the Tsuneko and Reiji Okazaki Award, "in honor of the spirit and legacy of Professors Okazaki."<ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.itbm.nagoya-u.ac.jp/okazaki_award/|title=Tsuneko & Reiji Okazaki Award|website=www.itbm.nagoya-u.ac.jp|access-date=2017-10-31}}</ref>

In 2015, she was elected as a [[Person of Cultural Merit]].<ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.isen.ac.jp/nagoya/mind/special/detail.html?id=16649|title=T.O.L.講義：2015度の文化功労者に選ばれた、名古屋大学名誉教授 岡崎恒子先生による特別講義を実施しました！|website=isen.ac.jp|publisher=[[archive.is]]|date=2015-11-13|access-date=2017-10-31|url-status=dead|archiveurl=https://archive.today/20160315140355/http://www.isen.ac.jp/nagoya/mind/special/detail.html?id=16649|archivedate=2016-03-15}}</ref>

In 2021, she received the [[Order of Culture]].<ref>{{cite web |url= https://www.jiji.com/jc/article?k=2021102600557&g=pol|title= 長嶋茂雄さんら9人文化勲章 功労者に加山雄三さんら|access-date= October 26, 2021|work= Jiji.com|language=ja}}</ref>
